title: ETF vs Mutual Fund: What Is the Difference?
summary: ETF vs mutual fund in plain terms: what the two fund types share, how buying, pricing and fees differ, what changes in a taxable account, and what to check before comparing them.
body_markdown:
Start with the overlap, because it is bigger than most comparison tables suggest. The SEC staff's[investor bulletin on mutual funds and ETFs](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/characteristics-mutual-funds-exchange-traded-funds) lists the shared features: both register with the SEC and publish a prospectus, both pool money from many investors into one portfolio, both are typically managed by SEC-registered investment advisers, and both can follow a passive index strategy or an active one. Both also charge fees and expenses regardless of how the fund performs.


Neither one is insured. Investor.gov's[ETF page](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/mutual-funds-and-exchange-traded-2) and[mutual fund page](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/mutual-funds-and-exchange-traded-1) both state that these funds are not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any other government agency, and that you can lose some or all of the money you invest.


Diversification is shared too, with a limit. The bulletin notes that some funds are less diverse than others, and that some ETFs track the performance of a single stock. You also cannot always tell the fund type from its name: some ETFs leave “ETF” out, and some exchange-traded products that are not registered funds use it. The bulletin points to the investment strategy section of the prospectus, which you can get free from the SEC's EDGAR database or from the fund.
